video_title: From Wet Lab to RL Env: 10,000 Drug-Discovery Campaigns in a Weekend — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
gist: Ian Quigley (CEO, Leash Bio) explains how ~10-person Leash uses DNA-encoded library screens (about 2,000 protein constructs, ~5,000 screens, 6.5M+ molecules each, plus engineered pocket mutants) to build physically grounded small-molecule binding data, after showing public ChEMBL data mostly encodes chemist 'sociology' and that no Kaggle team beat chance on novel chemistry. Leash now turns its database into an instant-feedback RL environment for language-model agents (10,000+ SAR campaigns in a weekend) and is pursuing spinouts from selective hits on ~700 targets.

themes.theme: Clever Hans: public chem data learns sociology

insights.claim: A classifier trained on ChEMBL molecules from 1,815 prolific chemists (30+ papers, 600+ molecules) identified the creating chemist from molecular structure alone with 60% top-5 accuracy.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Public med-chem datasets carry strong author-style fingerprints that models can exploit instead of learning chemistry.
insights.quote: It's 1,815 chemists. And then we trained a classifier to predict a chemist from looking at the molecule alone. And we got a top five accuracy of [music] 60%.

insights.claim: Representing molecules only as a ~1,800-element vector of 'probability of creator' predicts ChEMBL activity as well as using chemical structure, and combining the two adds little, implying activity models on public data mostly learn sociology rather than physics.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Models trained on public binding data (a field standard for PhDs and startups) may have little real chemical understanding; diligence any AI-chem company relying on it.
insights.quote: We really think that it's learning a lot of sociology. It's not learning ground truth.

insights.claim: Chemist fingerprints arise because medicinal chemists make many unrecorded choices about what not to make (cost, synthesizability, superstition about favorite building blocks), and those omissions imprint on what does get made and tested.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Absence of counterfactual/negative data in pharma records is a structural flaw, not just noise.
insights.quote: not making that choice is a fingerprint that that is going to land on what does get made

insights.claim: Even companies generating their own internal data are likely exposed to the authorship bias, because their multiple chemists have distinctive styles and apply them to different projects.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Proprietary pharma data moats may be less valuable for ML than assumed unless experimentally designed to remove selection bias.
insights.quote: if you are generating your own data, then you are probably victim to this because your organization probably has multiple chemists who have their own distinctive chemical styles

insights.claim: In public datasets, molecular weight alone is among the strongest predictors of binding (e.g., tying for first in CASP16), because chemists keep adding groups to molecules that already work, an artifact of the data rather than chemistry.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Brandon Anderson)
insights.so_what: Benchmarks on public data can be gamed by trivial baselines; claimed AI wins need artifact-controlled evals.
insights.quote: all you have to do is sort by molecular weight. That's like one of the single [laughter] single biggest predictors you can possibly have.

insights.claim: For its Kaggle competition Leash released about 4 billion physical small-molecule/protein interactions, measured by one person in Quigley's basement, versus just under 3 million in BindingDB, then the largest aggregated public binding database.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Pooled DEL screening can generate data three orders of magnitude beyond public corpora at tiny cost.
insights.quote: we released a data set that was about four billion physical interactions and it was all measured by a single person in the basement of my house.

insights.claim: In Leash's Kaggle competition (~2,000 teams, 3 well-studied protein targets, a 130M-molecule triazine-core library from AlphaMa sponsor), no team beat chance on the hardest held-out split using a totally different Leash-designed library with no shared hub or building blocks.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Current ML small-molecule binding prediction does not generalize to novel chemistry; a large white space remains.
insights.quote: And then when you go to the most challenging eval, no one did better than chance.

insights.claim: Three of the top five Kaggle finishers were variants of the noisy tutorial notebook, and the winner (Victor Schlapov) also performed no better than chance on the hardest split.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Sophisticated modeling gave little edge; data, not architecture, is the bottleneck.
insights.quote: three of the top five uh were the noisy tutorial notebook.

insights.claim: Leash gave roughly a 5% chance that co-folding approaches plus its 1000x-larger dataset would solve the problem and obviate the company; it did not happen, which the team read as validation to scale data collection.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Founders treated a public contest as a cheap existential test of their moat before committing a decade.
insights.quote: we gave it about a 5% chance that recent advancements and kind of like coalfolding approaches would mean that it would obiate our company entirely.

insights.claim: Simple SMILES strings beat fancier molecular representations (3D graphs, spherical convolutional nets) in the Kaggle competition, though not by a resounding margin.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Supports a bitter-lesson, data-first strategy over bespoke chemistry-informed architectures.
insights.quote: the thing that we were doing which are just basic smiles kind of beat everything else.

insights.claim: Leash describes itself as 'extremely bitter lesson pilled': if a scalable measurement regime yields good signal, the right move is to collect massive data, and the contest's difficulty was a signal to 'pour gas' on data generation.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Strategy is a data-scaling bet; value accrues to whoever owns the scalable, clean measurement engine.
insights.quote: like we we are extremely bitter lesson pill over here.

insights.claim: All Kaggle competition data, including evals, was released openly on Polaris (a nonprofit run by Recursion) to challenge skeptics who argued only weak teams competed; no one has yet performed well on it.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Open benchmark remains unsolved; a clear yardstick for any claimed generalizable binding model.
insights.quote: it is all on Polaris which is like a nonprofit group that was run by recursion.

themes.theme: DEL engine: scale, cost, and data strategy

insights.claim: Arrayed one-compound-per-well libraries max out in the low single-digit millions, while the largest DNA-encoded library ever built contains 40 trillion molecules.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: DELs offer orders-of-magnitude more measurement throughput than traditional HTS for small-molecule binding.
insights.quote: With Dell's, the largest one that has been produced um is 40 trillion molecules.

insights.claim: Leash's 'party line' is that there are only two scalable readouts in life-science ML: taking pictures and DNA sequencing (itself a form of pictures); Quigley argues proteomics is not yet at scale.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Bio-ML platforms built on imaging or sequencing readouts have structural scalability advantages over proteomics-based ones.
insights.quote: There's really only really only one scalable technology in town and that technology is taking pictures. Sequencing DNA is another way of taking pictures.

insights.claim: Sequencing cost declines plateaued for a while but new entrants are driving prices down again, and Leash explicitly plans its data-collection scale around that trajectory.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Cheaper sequencing directly lowers Leash-style DEL screening costs, a tailwind for sequencing-readout biotechs.
insights.quote: now a bunch of new companies have started up and they're driving it down again.

insights.claim: Leash has developed and screened about 2,000 protein constructs across roughly 5,000 screens, each against at least 6.5 million molecules, likely the most mutant screening of anyone; a one-off CRO DEL screen would cost about $100K each.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Implies Leash produced data worth hundreds of millions at CRO prices on modest capital, a big cost advantage.
insights.quote: we have uh developed and screened about 2,000 different protein constructs. um a total of probably about 5,000 screens in the history of the company across at least 6 and a half million molecules each.

insights.claim: Leash has only about 10 employees, has not raised much money, and screens up to 100 protein constructs per week on big weeks.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Extreme capital efficiency; small team running a high-throughput platform.
insights.quote: if you're going to be out screening a 100 protein constructs a week, which is what we do on big weeks

insights.claim: Leash chose to better characterize smaller libraries across many proteins rather than use ever-larger libraries against few targets, since a 100M-compound library helped less than deeper characterization under a fixed budget.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Data diversity across the protein axis matters more than raw library size for generalizable models.
insights.quote: this 100 million compound library that didn't help as much to us as better characterizing a smaller one.

insights.claim: Traditional DEL users are traumatized because they screen one hard target after months of protein prep, push for giant libraries, and never characterize library quirks; screening each library against hundreds of targets reveals manufacturing artifacts and even protein production problems.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Leash's edge comes from usage pattern (many targets per library), not just DEL chemistry itself.
insights.quote: every one of our chemical libraries gets screened against many hundreds of targets.

insights.claim: Leash uses 32 or 48 distinct DNA barcodes per molecule to detect proteins that bind DNA rather than the small molecule, and has discovered proteins not previously described as DNA binders.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Built-in controls make DEL data more trustworthy as ML training data.
insights.quote: we have 32 or 48 different barcodes all encoding this one small molecule.

insights.claim: When off-DNA resynthesized, about 90% of easy-target DEL hits and about 50% of hard-target hits still work in functional assays, and replicate screens months apart return the same hits in roughly the same order.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Quantifies DEL hit-translation attrition and reproducibility.
insights.quote: for things that are easy in our hands about 90% of them work for things that are hard is about 50

insights.claim: Arrayed compound library labels are typically wrong 20 to 30% of the time when audited, a mislabeling problem Quigley says is comparable to or worse than in DELs.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Undercuts the common assumption that arrayed HTS data is cleaner than DEL data.
insights.quote: they're typically off by 20 to 30%. It's an enormous mislabeling problem.

themes.theme: Engineered activity cliffs and mutant screens

insights.claim: Hermes, Leash's simple model (ESM protein embedding plus a SMILES next-token chemistry embedding joined with cross-attention, predicting binary binding), held steady across increasingly strict building-block-cluster splits while XGBoost degraded steadily.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Rigorous splits separate genuine generalization from memorization; XGBoost is a mandatory baseline.
insights.quote: we compared that to the Hermes performance, which was pretty steady across all these different regimes.

insights.claim: Trained exclusively on internal Leash data, Hermes was benchmarked on ~13 million public tests across ~500 protein targets and performed roughly on par with Boltz on the binding task.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Internal-only DEL data generalizes to external chemical space at roughly SOTA level, supporting the data moat claim.
insights.quote: I think it's like 13 million or something across like many it's like 500 protein target.

insights.claim: On BRD4, Boltz was perfect on a molecule that also appeared in PDB crystal structures it had almost certainly trained on, while Hermes did poorly, which Leash reads as evidence of memorization in structural models.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Co-folding benchmark results may be inflated by train/test leakage.
insights.quote: Boltz was perfect at it. And it's because we suspect that Boltz had seen this protein and this individual molecule in a crystal structure already

insights.claim: State-of-the-art co-folding models, when a protein pocket is digitally broken (filled in or removed via sequence changes), still place the small molecule where the pocket used to be, suggesting they memorize rather than understand physics.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Structure-based AI drug design has a physics-understanding gap that experimental negative data could fill.
insights.quote: it will shove the small molecule in where the pocket used to be.

insights.claim: Hermes attention maps showed the model focusing on short, non-conserved amino-acid stretches away from binding pockets, effectively memorizing a 'nickname' for each protein; adding engineered mutant screens made attention spread across residues evenly.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Interpretability can diagnose memorization, and targeted data (mutants) can fix it.
insights.quote: Hermes was probably coming up with a nickname for the protein.

insights.claim: Leash physically mutates binding-pocket residues and rescreens, combined with competition assays using known ligands, to generate true negatives and map which molecular groups interact with which residues; the combinatorial library yields multiple independent chemical series showing the same shift.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Creates causal, physically grounded negative data that public structural datasets lack.
insights.quote: we thought one way to go get around this is to experimentally engineer mutations in binding regions of these proteins and then rescreening.

insights.claim: Leash aspires to screen every human protein and then non-human orthologs, partly to predict species-specific behavior such as whether to run a mouse versus rat model.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Broad proteome coverage could extend into off-target toxicity and preclinical species selection.
insights.quote: It is it is not at all an exaggeration to say that it is our aspiration to have screened every protein

insights.claim: Quigley's real moat against a better-funded lab out-scaling Leash is process culture: years of catching cheating modes, batch effects and metadata tracking from Recursion and Leash, e.g., using lumacaftor-like library compounds as a flag for misfolded protein batches.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Moat is tacit operational know-how, not capital; replication takes time rather than money.
insights.quote: if we get a bunch of lumac heads that protein probably didn't fall fold right.

insights.claim: Leash is training open-source language models (Qwen, GLM) to describe molecules in plain English and run hypothesis-driven SAR campaigns against its existing screening database as an instant-feedback RL environment, much like a coding sandbox.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Turns wet-lab data into a scalable, physically grounded RL environment, a rare asset for reasoning-model training.
insights.quote: It will get back the answer instantly like it's a coding sandbox and then it will update its hypothesis about the binding.

insights.claim: A medicinal chemist sees maybe a couple dozen to 50 SAR campaigns in a career; Leash generated over 10,000 such campaigns in one weekend without trying hard.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Massive scaling of med-chem experience data for training reasoning agents.
insights.quote: you might see a couple dozen of these, maybe 50 of these in your career. >> And so right now, you know, last weekend we pulled out >> over 10,000 of them.

insights.claim: Given 10 binders and 10 non-binders and a budget of 100 molecule queries, Leash's agents find the best binders out of 6.5 million molecules.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Early evidence of agentic molecular optimization efficiency in silico.
insights.quote: they'll get the best binders out of six and a half million in that budget.

insights.claim: Natural language acts as a regularizer that resists memorization better than scaling Hermes-style models, which would eventually memorize the mutants too; Leash knows of no other physically grounded RL loop this scalable and fast.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Positions DEL data as differentiated RL infrastructure versus robotic lab-in-the-loop efforts that are slower and resource limited.
insights.quote: we are unaware of other problems where you have a reinforcement learning loop that is physically grounded that is this scalable this fast.

insights.claim: Because Leash measures all molecules across all proteins, its data includes counterfactual choices a human chemist would not have made, which agents need to learn without inheriting chemist sociology.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Unbiased exhaustive measurement is the key differentiator over pharma historical data.
insights.quote: It's got to have the counterfactuals. It's got to make mistakes

insights.claim: If models master chemical reasoning, Leash expects to enter agriculture, veterinary science and materials science without screening in those domains, and eventually no longer need screening at all.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Option value beyond pharma; answer to the 'why do you need ML if you have data' business-model critique.
insights.quote: we can run off and go work in agriculture like immediately right you could go work in veterinary science you go work off material science

insights.claim: Leash went from DEL hits to good PK/PD in mice in 6 months with few med-chem cycles on an inflammation compound, with cytokine biomarkers in mouse blood moving as expected; libraries were designed with drug-likeness and ADMET scores in the optimization function.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Early in vivo validation that DEL-derived, ML-designed chemistry can be drug-like.
insights.quote: we've gone directly from uh from chemical library hits to good PKPD in a mouse in 6 months

insights.claim: Leash has selective-looking starting chemical matter for around 700 targets and is talking with partners to spin up new entities to advance some assets.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Business model includes spinouts/partnerships monetizing a large proprietary hit portfolio.
insights.quote: right now we have starting material that looks pretty selective to us for uh I think like 700 targets

insights.claim: A key commercial target is oral small molecules replacing injectable antibodies for cytokine-driven inflammatory indications, avoiding infusion and cold-chain logistics; Leash says it has selective material for many cytokines.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Oral alternatives to biologics in inflammation are a large value-capture opportunity and a threat to antibody incumbents.
insights.quote: going after a small molecule therapeutic that you could take as a pill instead of an infusion, one that doesn't require uh, like cold chain

insights.claim: Quigley argues protein-drug ML (antibody companies such as Isomorphic, Chai, Nabla) works because protein data is ample, but comparable capabilities do not yet exist for small molecules, which is Leash's founding thesis.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Small-molecule AI is the less-crowded, data-starved frontier relative to biologics AI.
insights.quote: Um our thesis is that uh those capabilities are really not here for small molecule approaches.

insights.claim: Early discovery is a 'lamppost problem': it is where scalable measurement is possible today (no million-mouse or million-phase-1 experiments), so ML will move up layers of biological abstraction over time.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Explains why AI-bio value is concentrated in early discovery despite it being a small share of drug costs.
insights.quote: It is a little bit of a lampost problem where the things where we can make enough scalable measurements in the life sciences are these early problems.

insights.claim: Newer DNA-compatible chemistries over the past ~four years give carbon-carbon and carbon-nitrogen bonds beyond digestible amide links, so Quigley worries more about limited commercial building-block diversity and custom synthesis than about DEL linkage stability.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Building-block supply and custom synthesis are the scaling constraint for DEL chemical space.
insights.quote: I'm more worried about building block diversity uh than there sources for that.

insights.claim: Leash can reliably rank relative potency from DEL reads but cannot yet translate reads into Kd values, and is exploring SPR-based potency ladders.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Affinity quantification remains a gap in DEL-based ML data.
insights.quote: I think translating it into KDS is something that we're actively working on

insights.claim: Quigley's by-fiat bottleneck wish is massively parallel, high-quality small-molecule purification (beyond HPLC), enabling clean orthogonal validation of DEL measurements at scale.
insights.speaker: Ian Quigley (Leash Bio CEO)
insights.so_what: Parallel purification tooling is an underserved market for chemistry automation.
insights.quote: being able to like clean up stuff at a massive scale would be really really nice
